messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 31
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Journalist
- Trauma Type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
- Pcl5: 78

She is 31, a South Eastern Asian woman who works as a journalist, and when she tells the story now, she does it the way she has learned to do many difficult things in her job: in sequence, with details, as if getting the facts right might somehow contain what happened. Before her life split into before and after, she is married, busy, and often tired in the ordinary way. She and her younger brother text almost every day. He sends her voice notes full of jokes, links to strange local news stories, and reminders that she works too hard. Even after her divorce, when her life feels less anchored, he is the person she still calls without thinking.

The call about his death comes on a weekday while she is at the newsroom, editing a piece under deadline. A relative’s number flashes on her phone, and she ignores it at first, then answers on the third try with irritation already in her voice. She remembers the sound that comes through the line before she understands the words: screaming, confusion, someone saying there has been an accident, someone else saying he is gone. She keeps asking, “What hospital?” because her mind cannot make room for death until she has ruled out rescue. She hears herself speaking sharply, almost professionally, demanding names, times, locations. Later she feels ashamed of that tone, but at the time it is the only way she can remain upright.

In the first days after, she moves as if assigned a role she must perform. She books travel, speaks to police, answers relatives, helps arrange the funeral. People praise her for being strong. She hates hearing it. At night she sees images she never witnessed: her brother alone, frightened, calling for help. She tries to replace them with real memories of him, but the imagined final moments intrude with a force that feels violent. She sleeps in fragments, waking with her heart pounding, disoriented and soaked in sweat. Sometimes she jolts awake hearing her phone ring, only to realize the room is silent.

When she returns to work, she expects routine to steady her. Instead, journalism becomes another place where grief ambushes her. Sirens in the street make her freeze at her desk. Breaking-news alerts send a shock through her body before she even reads them. She is assigned a story about a fatal road accident and feels her throat close while interviewing a witness. She keeps her notebook open and her face composed, but afterward she locks herself in the bathroom and vomits. From then on, she starts swapping assignments whenever she can, pretending she is overloaded or already committed. She tells colleagues she is focusing on political reporting now, but privately she is trying to avoid any mention of sudden death, hospitals, emergency responders, mourning families.

Outside work, her world narrows. She stops answering friends who say she needs to get out of the apartment. She cannot bear the bright, casual cruelty of normal conversation. If someone complains about a sibling, she goes cold and distant. Family gatherings become unbearable because every meal carries the shape of his absence. She watches her mother’s face for signs of fresh collapse and feels responsible for holding everyone together, yet she resents them too, especially when they ask her to retell what officials said. She has memorized every fact around his death and returns to them compulsively, reading old messages, checking timelines, scrolling through photographs late into the night until dawn light enters the room.

Her divorce, once a painful but manageable loss, now takes on a different meaning. She begins to think everyone leaves suddenly, either by choice or by force. She no longer trusts good moments. If she laughs with a colleague over coffee, a thought arrives immediately after: this can disappear in a second. She startles when people touch her unexpectedly. She sits near exits in restaurants and scans crowds without deciding to. On public transport she studies strangers’ faces, bracing for bad news that has not yet happened. She says she feels “on assignment” all the time, as though some part of her is permanently gathering evidence against safety.

There are stretches when she feels almost nothing. She speaks, writes, files stories, pays bills, and answers emails with mechanical competence, then goes home and sits in the dark scrolling through her brother’s old voice notes. She has not deleted his number. Sometimes she opens the chat window just to see his name at the top of the screen. She still expects, in some irrational corner of herself, that a new message will arrive.

Now, months later, she looks composed to most people. She is productive enough to pass at work and articulate enough to explain what happened. But her life is organized around avoidance, vigilance, and the exhausting effort to outrun images that return uninvited. She says the world no longer feels tragic in a philosophical sense; it feels actively unsafe, intimate in its danger. The hardest part, she says, is that she used to believe that if she paid close attention, she could understand events and tell them clearly. Her brother’s death has broken that faith. She is left with facts, and none of them make him less gone.
